analysis.one_liner: Taxes large corporations 40% on profits they stockpile instead of spending or hiring.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a vote and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: During a period of high unemployment, the bill would have placed a temporary 40% surtax on domestic corporations with large retained earnings — charging them on any increase in profits they held onto beyond their average for the prior three years. Corporations with retained earnings under $5 million were exempt, as were firms legally required to hold reserves and companies too new to have a three-year track record. The goal was to pressure large companies to put cash to work — through hiring, investment, or shareholder payouts — and the revenue raised would have gone to deficit reduction [S3] [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Job seekers and workers, if the tax pressure pushed large corporations to deploy hoarded profits into hiring or investment; and the general public, through the deficit reduction the revenue was designated for [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposed a 40% surtax on domestic corporations for 2011 and 2012 on the excess of their retained earnings over their average retained earnings for the preceding three years [S3].
Corporations with retained earnings below $5 million in a year, those required by federal law to build reserves, and those not in existence for the full three-year base period were exempt [S3].
Revenue raised was required to be deposited in the Treasury and used to reduce the federal deficit or debt [S3].
The bill's stated premise — reflected in its title — was that corporate assets should be used to hire workers, and it arrived during a period of high unemployment [S1] [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large domestic corporations with more than $5 million in retained earnings, which would owe a 40% tax on earnings growth beyond their recent three-year average for tax years 2011 and 2012 [S3].

drawbacks.text: The tax measured retained earnings against a three-year average, so a corporation recovering from losses or a small firm building its first cushion above $5 million could owe the surtax even if it was hoarding nothing [S3].
Corporations could avoid the tax by paying dividends or buying back stock rather than hiring, so the tax would not reliably produce jobs — it would only reliably produce revenue or payouts [S3].
The surtax applied only to tax years beginning in 2011 or 2012, making it a short-window intervention whose effect on hiring plans, which take longer to arrange, was uncertain [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax gave large corporations a real financial reason to move accumulated profits out of reserves during a weak job market, and its revenue was earmarked for deficit reduction. But its design was blunt: it taxed rising retained earnings whether or not a firm had hiring needs, and firms could satisfy it with buybacks or dividends rather than jobs. An honest supporter would call it a two-year pressure tool, not a jobs program.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee took no further action on it before the Congress ended in January 2013 [S5].

narrative.text: Representative Michael Capuano introduced the bill on September 22, 2011, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1] [S5].
The bill attracted one cosponsor, a Democrat; no further cosponsors and no committee or floor action followed [S4] [S5].
No action was recorded after the referral, and the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, with the bill still in committee [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations that retained growing earnings through 2011 and 2012 did so without the 40% surtax, and the Treasury forwent the revenue the bill would have directed to deficit reduction.

for.name: Rep. Michael Capuano
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means; it was one of his proposals to push companies sitting on cash to hire.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no markup, no hearing on the bill, no floor report — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and a single Democratic cosponsor with no recorded Republican support, and it never reached a vote, so the parties' full positions were never tested.

industries.industry: Large domestic corporations (retained earnings over $5 million)
industries.note: For 2011 and 2012 the bill would have taxed 40% of their retained-earnings growth beyond a three-year average, unless they deployed the money into payouts, investment, or reserves required by law. Corporate treasurers' preference for holding cash ran against the bill's goal of pushing that money toward wages and deficit reduction [S3].
They were exempt from the surtax entirely, giving them relative cost advantages over the large corporations that would have paid it [S3].
